title: Something understood
hookLine: Herbert's poem Prayer ends with a list of images and "something understood" (Prayer I)
tomorrow: a man bangs the table and shouts no more. what calls him back?

lines: TWO PLAIN WORDS AT THE END.
cards: Ask around what prayer is, and the answers scatter: asking for things, talking to God, sitting quietly, saying old words together. George Herbert didn't write a definition. He wrote a list.
Prayer, the Church's banquet. God's breath in man returning to his birth. On and on, image after image, and then it ends with two plain words: something understood.

teach.b: Here's the question under the list: what is prayer?
Herbert's answer is a sonnet that never once says prayer is. It only piles up names. "The soul in paraphrase, heart in pilgrimage."
Reversed thunder. A kind of tune.
"Heaven in ordinary, man well drest." Church bells heard beyond the stars. And after all that: "something understood."
The teaching inside is Christian: prayer is God's own breath going back to God, and for Herbert it runs through Christ; the poem even names the spear in Christ's side.
Walton tells that when Herbert rang his church bell for daily prayer, some of the farmers would stop their plows and pray where they stood. A neighbor tradition asks it too.

teach.h: THE TALMUD: SERVICE OF THE HEART.
teach.b: The Talmud reads the command to serve God with all your heart and asks: what service happens in the heart? It answers: prayer.
Shared: prayer as something the heart does, more than the lips.
Honestly different: Jewish prayer keeps fixed daily services, traditionally in Hebrew, best said with a minyan; Herbert's Anglican prayer runs through Christ and the Book of Common Prayer.

how: Anglicans pray daily morning and evening prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, and Herbert's Prayer (I) is read as a meditation on it. Jews pray fixed daily services, ideally with a minyan, which the Talmud calls the service of the heart.

s: Herbert's poem Prayer gives a one-line definition
it never says 'prayer is'; it piles up images and ends 'something understood.'
the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart
the rabbis read 'serve him with all your heart' as prayer.
Jewish and Christian prayer are the same thing in different words
both speak of the heart; the ways differ: fixed daily services, prayer through Christ.

games.q: a Jewish friend says prayer is "the service of the heart." how does that sit with Herbert's poem?
o: close: both make prayer a matter of the heart, and the ways differ.
identical: so the two traditions are basically the same.
nothing in common: Herbert's prayer is poetry, hers is rules.
games.why: the Talmud calls prayer service of the heart; Herbert calls it heart in pilgrimage. shared heart; different ways: fixed daily services, prayer through Christ.

practice: Write a short list poem about prayer, or about quiet if prayer isn't yours: three or four images, no explaining. A kitchen at night. A held breath.
A bell. End it, if you like, the way Herbert did, with something plain.

wordCard.voice: Something understood: the last two words of Herbert's list, the plainest after all the images.

orig.note: Hebrew (the Talmud): the service of the heart, the rabbis' name for prayer. Today's neighbor word.

carryVoice: Your line: something understood. Not explained, only understood. Just one more day in this camp.
